newsitem.title: INDIA: U.S. considers reward over Kashmir hostages.
newsitem.headline: U.S. considers reward over Kashmir hostages.

text.p: The United States is considering offering a financial reward for information about four Westerners taken hostage by separatist guerrillas in Kashmir more than a year ago, diplomats said on Tuesday.
The money would come from a U.S. government programme which offers up to $2 million for information that can be used to combat acts of "terrorism" aimed at U.S. citizens abroad, they said.
"The purpose is to locate the hostages and apprehend those responsible," a spokesman for the U.S. Embassy in New Delhi said.

Washington has not yet approached India about the idea, and will seek the backing of New Delhi as well as the three other countries whose nationals were kidnapped 15 months ago before offering the reward, diplomats said.
Americans Donald Hutchings and John Childs, and Britons Keith Mangan and Paul Wells were kidnapped by Al-Faran militants while trekking in the Kashmiri mountains on July 4, 1995.
Childs escaped four days later, and Al-Faran captured Norwegian Hans Christian Ostroe and German Dirk Hasert. A month later, Ostroe was found beheaded in a remote Kashmiri forest.

Negotiations between Indian officials and Al-Faran broke down last November. The four remaining hostages have since been sighted from time to time by local Kashmiris including nomadic shepherds, but authorities have not been able to determine with certainty whether the captives are dead or alive.
Earlier this year, experts using sniffer dogs scoured a forest where a captured militant said he believed the four hostages had been buried. No traces of the men were found.

"Before we move forward, we need the agreement of the quad (British, German, Norwegian) partners and India. We need to feel that all nations involved and the host government agree that this is an effective strategy," the U.S. Embassy spokesman said.
Unknown before the kidnappings, Al-Faran is among dozens of of groups fighting Indian rule in Jammu and Kashmir state.

India claims Al-Faran is linked to Pakistan-based Harkat-ul-Ansar, and accuses Islamabad of arming and training militants. Pakistan, which rules over one third of Kashmir and has staked a claim to the rest, denies the accusation.

U.S. diplomats said the reward would not amount to ransom as it would not be paid to anyone associated with the kidnappings. "This is not a ransom. There will be no reward paid to those who took part in the kidnappings," a diplomat said.
Officials acknowledged that the idea of a reward reflected a frustration with efforts to locate the hostages and a desire to examine other options.

"We have exhausted every other possibility," the U.S. Embassy spokesman said. "This is an idea we have been mulling for a long time. We want to see if now is the proper moment to come forward with it."

U.S. diplomats said they did not want a reward to send a signal that armed groups in Kashmir could search for the hostages and their captors. "It is not a green light to engage in illegal acts," a diplomat said.

U.S. officials said that while the reward programme, under the Justice Department but administered overseas by the State Department, provides for up to $2 million in individual cases, they did not expect that much to be offered in this instance.
The wife of U.S. hostage Donald Hutchings, Jane Schelly, was expected to come to India from the United States in mid-October in hopes of gaining information about the hostages, diplomats said.
